text: Munich. The World Cup final. Barely a minute has gone, and West Germany haven't even touched the ball.
Johan Cruyff runs into the penalty area — and is brought down. Penalty.
A twenty-two-year-old midfielder walks up to take it. In the biggest game in the world, he doesn't place it. He smashes it, straight down the middle.
It's the first penalty ever scored in a World Cup final. And the man who took it was about to become a Barcelona player. His name was Johan Neeskens.
Barcelona already had a Johan. Neeskens became the other one.
This is his story, told the way he lived it — in pictures.
Part one. The boy who ran.
Neeskens grew up in Heemstede, near Haarlem, and came to Ajax as a teenager. Rinus Michels saw something in him that had nothing to do with elegance.
He never stopped running. He pressed, he tackled, he chased players twice his age — and then, with the ball, he could play.
At nineteen, he was a starter in the best team in Europe. Michels even used him at right-back, so his energy could be everywhere.
In June nineteen seventy-one, at Wembley, Ajax won their first European Cup.
Next to Johan Cruyff, Neeskens looked like the opposite: Cruyff the thinker, Neeskens the engine. Together, they were the heart of total football.
Ajax won the European Cup again in nineteen seventy-two, and again in nineteen seventy-three. Three in a row.
Look at the pictures from those years and you notice something. Neeskens is almost always in the air — jumping, diving, flying into tackles.
He played as if every ball was the last ball of the game.
And he became the man for penalties. He had one rule: hit it hard and don't think. Goalkeepers who guessed a corner had no chance.
Part two. The summer of nineteen seventy-four.
At the World Cup in West Germany, the Netherlands played a football the world had never seen. Neeskens was everywhere.
Crowds followed the team from the moment they arrived. Everyone wanted the two Johans.
Neeskens was kicked, knocked down, injured — and he kept getting back up.
He scored against Bulgaria, East Germany and Brazil. Five goals in the tournament, from midfield.
Against Brazil, he was kicked so hard that he lay unconscious on the grass. The Brazilian defender was sent off — and Neeskens played on.
Then came the final, and that penalty. One–nil to the Netherlands after two minutes.
But West Germany came back. A penalty of their own, then a goal from Gerd Müller just before half-time. Two–one. That was how it ended.
The team that had changed football did not win the World Cup.
And yet, the next day in Amsterdam, they were welcomed home like champions. People had seen something they would never forget.
Part three. Barcelona.
Nine days after the final, Neeskens got married in his home town.
Two days after that, he and his wife boarded a plane. Destination: Barcelona.
He was reuniting with his old coach, Rinus Michels, and with his old team-mate, Johan Cruyff. Barça had just won their first league title in fourteen years.
The supporters at the Camp Nou now had two Johans. They gave the new one a name in Catalan: Johan Segon. Johan the Second.
For five seasons, he gave Barça what he had given Ajax: energy, aggression, goals from midfield, and a refusal to give up.
Supporters loved him for it. He wasn't as graceful as Cruyff, but he fought for every ball as if the shirt was his own skin.
In nineteen seventy-eight, Barça won the Spanish Cup.

And in May nineteen seventy-nine, in Basel, they won their first European Cup Winners' Cup, four–three against Fortuna Düsseldorf after extra time. That summer, Neeskens left for America and the New York Cosmos.
Part four. The second final.
Four years after Munich, the Netherlands reached another World Cup final, in Argentina — this time without Cruyff. Neeskens was still there.
They lost again, three–one after extra time, to the hosts.
Two finals, two defeats. It's one of football's great injustices that the team of total football never won the trophy.
Neeskens played on for years, in America, and later back in Europe. He never really stopped running.
Part five. Coming home.

As a coach, he worked alongside Guus Hiddink, and in two thousand and six he came back to Barcelona as Frank Rijkaard's assistant — in the dugout at the Camp Nou, where the supporters still remembered Johan Segon.
In October twenty twenty-four, Johan Neeskens died in Algeria, where he was working on a coaching project for young coaches. He was seventy-three.
Barcelona, Ajax and the whole of Dutch football paid tribute to one of their greatest.
He was never the most famous Johan. But in every photo from those years, there he is — in the air, in the tackle, in the middle of everything. The other Johan.
Whose story should we tell in pictures next? Tell me in the comments.
